title: The Button Has Betrayed You
description: Your first Forge investigation starts with a button that refuses to do what you expect. Instead of guessing, you will observe the failure, gather browser evidence, test a hypothesis, make a targeted fix, and verify what actually changed.

objectives.statement: Distinguish directly observable browser behavior from assumptions about what caused it.
Use browser evidence to investigate an unexpected interface behavior instead of guessing.
Connect an observed runtime failure to a plausible cause, targeted fix, and verified result.
Explain a frontend failure as a causal chain from user action to browser behavior and eventual outcome.

content.title: The Button Has Betrayed You
content.hook: You have one job: save the changes. You click the button. Nothing happens.
content.context: This page is intentionally broken. Your first task is not to fix it. Your first task is to figure out what you actually know.
goals: Observe what the browser actually does.

feedback.correct: Good. We're investigating a system, not guessing at it.
feedback.incorrect: Nope. Don't solve it yet. Start with what you can actually observe.

content.title: ACCOUNT SETTINGS
content.description: A tiny account settings interface containing a name field, an email field, a Save Changes button, and a status area that currently says nothing has been saved.

interactive.caption: Something is wrong. Don't fix it yet.

content.question: You click “Save Changes.” What should happen if the interface is working normally?

options.text: The status should indicate that the changes were saved.
The browser should close the page.
Nothing should happen because buttons never change page state.
The HTML source file should automatically open.

content.explanation: The useful prediction is the expected observable behavior. We need that expectation before we can compare it with reality.

feedback.correct: Exactly. You now have an expectation you can test.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Define the behavior you expected to observe after the click.

hints.content: What visible change would tell you the save happened?

content.question: After clicking Save Changes and seeing nothing happen, which statements are directly observable?

options.text: The status text did not visibly change.
The JavaScript function is definitely missing.
The browser did not produce the result you expected.

content.explanation: Observable facts are evidence. Claims about the cause are hypotheses until we investigate them.

feedback.correct: There it is. You separated what happened from what you think caused it.
feedback.incorrect: Careful. Some options are explanations, not observations.

hints.content: Ask: could I know this just by looking at what happened?
Anything containing “definitely” is probably a hypothesis rather than evidence.

content.prompt: Change the text inside the status element to “Testing the page.” Then look at the preview. Did the live page change?

content.instructions: Change only the status text. Run the page. Observe the preview. Do not worry about saving anything permanently.

testCases.description: The status text changes in the rendered page.

content.title: The Page You See Is Not the Source File
content.text: When a browser loads HTML, it creates a live representation of that document and uses it to produce the page you interact with. DevTools lets you inspect that live representation. Changes you make there can immediately affect what you see, but they do not magically rewrite the original source file.

callout.text: Think of DevTools as a place to experiment with the running page.

content.keyTakeaway: You can manipulate the live system to gather evidence without permanently changing the source.

content.question: The Save Changes button still does nothing. What is the most useful next investigation?

options.text: Inspect the button and look for evidence about how it behaves.
Change random CSS until something looks different.
Guess that the database is broken.

content.explanation: The best next step is the one that can reduce uncertainty and give you useful evidence.

feedback.incorrect: Not yet. Pick the action most likely to give you evidence about the failure.

hints.content: Choose the action that reveals information.
Random changes can change the symptom without explaining it.

content.title: Follow the Failure
content.description: A simple causal chain showing how a click becomes JavaScript execution and how a missing function causes the expected interface update to fail.

content.prompt: What should the status element contain after this code runs?
content.explanation: The function updates the status element with a new string, then the function is called.

feedback.correct: Correct. You're predicting behavior from the code instead of waiting for the browser to surprise you.
feedback.incorrect: Trace the function body. What does it assign to #status?

content.title: The Button Has Evidence
content.prompt: The button still fails. Use the browser evidence to identify the runtime problem, then make the smallest change that makes the save action update the status.
content.bugDescription: The save handler calls a function that does not exist.
hints: Don't guess yet. Look at the runtime error.
What name is JavaScript trying to find?
There is no saveChanges function defined in this code.
Make the handler update the status directly.
fixRequirements: The save action must no longer call an undefined function.
The status element must change to “Changes saved.”

content.prompt: The button wasn't really “broken.” Explain what caused the visible failure, from the click through to the missing status update.
guidelines: Start with what the user did.
Describe what JavaScript tried to do.
Explain why the expected UI change never happened.
content.sampleResponse: The click triggered the save handler. The handler tried to call saveChanges, but that function did not exist, so JavaScript threw a runtime error before the status could be updated.

content.title: One More Button
content.prompt: New page. New button. Same job: investigate before guessing. The Add Item button does nothing. Find the runtime problem, fix it, and verify that an item appears in the list.
content.bugDescription: The click handler calls a function that has not been defined.
hints: Start with the evidence. What does the runtime error say?
Look at the function name JavaScript is trying to resolve.
Create the list item directly inside the handler.
fixRequirements: The handler must no longer call an undefined function.
Clicking Add Item must add an item to the list.

content.title: What You Actually Did
takeaways: A visible failure is a symptom, not automatically the cause.
Good debugging starts by separating observations from assumptions.
A hypothesis should be tested against what the system actually does.
A fix is not finished until the behavior is verified.
Frontend engineering is partly the skill of figuring out what a system is actually doing.
nextSteps: Next, you will investigate the browser and the web platform more deliberately.
reviewQuestions: What was the first useful piece of evidence?
Why was the runtime error more useful than guessing about the CSS?

content.title: The Button Has Been Released From Custody
content.message: You didn't guess the answer. You observed a problem, collected evidence, tested a hypothesis, changed the system, and verified the result. That's debugging.
content.congratulations: Next time something breaks, your first move isn't “try random stuff.” It's “what do I actually know?”
